blocks.text: A hiker climbs steadily on a hot afternoon, her muscles releasing heat at several times their resting rate, and yet her core temperature stays within a degree or so of 37 degrees C. Her skin flushes, sweat appears and her breathing deepens. Nobody told her body to do any of that. A built-in control loop detected a rise in temperature and drove responses that pushed it back down; this unit shows how that loop is built.

blocks.markdown:
**Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a relatively constant internal environment, so that cells can work despite changes outside and inside the body. Variables such as core temperature, arterial pressure, plasma glucose and blood pH are held near particular values by regulatory systems. The variable being held is the **regulated variable**, and the value it is held near is the **set point**. Anything that pushes the variable away from its set point is a **perturbation** or disturbance (for example heat from exercise, a meal, or loss of blood).

Most homeostatic systems use **negative feedback**, in which a change in the regulated variable triggers a response that opposes the change. The loop has four stages. A **sensor** (receptor) detects the variable. An **integrator** (control centre) compares the signal with the set point and generates an error signal, the difference between what is sensed and what is wanted. An **effector** (muscle, gland or other target) carries out a response. The response alters the variable, which the sensor then detects again, closing the loop.

blocks.title: Components of a control loop
blocks.text: Sensor: detects the regulated variable. Afferent pathway: carries the information to the integrator. Integrator: compares the input with the set point and decides on a response. Efferent pathway: carries the command out. Effector: produces the response that opposes the perturbation. Error signal: the difference between the measured value and the set point.

blocks.title: Identifying the parts of a loop: thermoregulation
blocks.prompt: On a hot day core temperature rises slightly above 37 degrees C. Identify the sensor, integrator and effector, and explain how the response corrects the rise.

steps.text: Sensor: thermoreceptors in the skin and the core (including in the hypothalamus itself) detect the rise in temperature.
Integrator: the hypothalamus (preoptic area) compares the sensed temperature with the set point and finds it too high, producing an error signal.
Effectors: sweat glands (evaporation of sweat removes heat) and skin arterioles (vasodilation brings more blood to the skin, so more heat is lost to the environment). Heat production is also reduced.

Result: body heat loss increases, so temperature falls back towards 37 degrees C and the sensor input falls, ending the response. This is negative feedback because the response opposes the original change.

blocks.answer: Sensor: thermoreceptors. Integrator: hypothalamus. Effectors: sweat glands and skin arterioles. The response opposes the temperature rise.

blocks.caption: Mapping two regulated variables onto the loop components.
rows: Skin and core thermoreceptors, including hypothalamic neurons
Pancreatic beta cells sensing glucose directly
Beta cells respond in proportion to glucose (sensor and integrator combined)
Insulin acts on muscle, fat and liver
Glucose uptake and storage increase, plasma glucose falls

blocks.latex: G = \frac{\text{correction by feedback}}{\text{error remaining}} = \frac{\text{uncorrected change} - \text{remaining change}}{\text{remaining change}}
blocks.caption: Gain (G) of a negative feedback system: the larger the gain, the more completely the disturbance is corrected. Convention note: some textbooks define loop gain with a negative sign (for example G = -correction / error remaining) to show that the feedback opposes the error; here gain is quoted as a positive magnitude.

blocks.markdown: **Feedback is never perfect.** A negative feedback loop can only respond to an error that already exists, so some deviation always remains. The effectiveness is measured by the gain. If a disturbance would shift the variable by 10 units without regulation but the variable moves only 2 units with regulation, the feedback has corrected 8 units and left 2, so gain is 8 / 2 = 4. A high gain means the variable is held close to its set point. The set point itself can be changed deliberately: in fever, pyrogens act on the hypothalamus to raise the set point, so the body feels cold and generates heat (shivering, skin vasoconstriction) until the higher temperature is reached, and then defends it.

blocks.title: Calculating the gain of a loop
blocks.prompt: A heat load would raise core temperature by 4.0 degrees C if there were no regulation. With the thermoregulatory loop working, the rise is only 0.5 degrees C. Calculate the gain.

steps.text: Correction by feedback = uncorrected change - remaining change = 4.0 - 0.5 = 3.5 degrees C.
Interpretation: the loop removes seven times as much of the disturbance as remains, so temperature is tightly held, but not perfectly.

blocks.answer: Gain is 7: the feedback corrects most of the disturbance but leaves a small residual error of 0.5 degrees C.

blocks.caption: Negative and positive feedback compared.
rows: Stabilises the variable near a set point
Drives the variable away from the starting point until an event ends it
Thermoregulation; glucose regulation; arterial pressure control
Oxytocin and uterine contractions in labour; blood coagulation cascade

blocks.markdown: **Positive feedback.** In positive feedback the response reinforces the change that triggered it, so the deviation grows. It is not a homeostatic mechanism but a way of completing a process quickly. In late labour, stretching of the cervix by the baby's head sends signals to the hypothalamus, which triggers release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, which push the head further against the cervix and cause more stretch, and so more oxytocin. The loop ends when the baby is delivered and the stretch stimulus stops. In blood clotting, each activated clotting factor activates more factors, rapidly forming a clot at an injury site until the vessel wall is sealed.

items: A perturbation changes the regulated variable (the sensor detects a deviation).
Afferent signals travel to the integrator, which compares the input with the set point and generates an error signal.
Efferent signals drive effectors, which produce a response opposing the deviation.
The variable moves back towards the set point, the sensor signal falls and the response diminishes.

blocks.title: Negative feedback opposes; positive feedback amplifies
blocks.text: Do not judge feedback by whether the variable goes up or down: negative feedback is defined by the response opposing the perturbation, whether the variable was rising or falling. Positive feedback makes the deviation larger until an external event ends the cycle.

blocks.title: Set point versus normal range
blocks.text: A control system does not hold a variable at exactly the set point. It reduces the deviation, leaving a residual error, and some variables change with the time of day or are deliberately reset, as in fever. Do not assume that a changed value means the control system has failed.

points: Homeostasis keeps regulated variables near set points using control loops with a sensor, an integrator and an effector.
In negative feedback the response opposes the perturbation; in positive feedback it amplifies it and ends only when an external event stops the cycle.
Gain measures effectiveness: gain = (uncorrected change - remaining change) / remaining change (quoted as a positive magnitude), and feedback never corrects perfectly.
A perturbation is detected by sensors, compared with the set point by the integrator, and corrected by effectors, as in thermoregulation and plasma glucose control.

questions.stem: On a hot day the core temperature of a hiker rises. In the thermoregulatory negative feedback loop, which structure acts as the integrator?

options.text: The hypothalamus
The sweat glands
Skin thermoreceptors
The skin arterioles

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the hypothalamus compares sensed temperature with the set point and generates the response.
distractorRationale.b: Sweat glands are effectors that produce the cooling response.
distractorRationale.c: Thermoreceptors are the sensors that detect temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Skin arterioles are effectors that increase heat loss by vasodilation.

questions.explanation: The integrator compares the input from the sensors with the set point and decides on a response. In thermoregulation this is the hypothalamus, while thermoreceptors are the sensors and sweat glands and skin arterioles are the effectors.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a physiological example of positive feedback?

options.text: Oxytocin release in late labour, where cervical stretch triggers more oxytocin and stronger contractions
Sweating when core temperature rises
Insulin release after a rise in plasma glucose
Shivering when core temperature falls

questions.correctOptionText: Oxytocin release in late labour, where cervical stretch triggers more oxytocin and stronger contractions

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the response (stronger contraction) increases the stimulus (cervical stretch), amplifying the change.
distractorRationale.b: Sweating lowers temperature, opposing the original rise: negative feedback.
distractorRationale.c: Insulin lowers glucose, opposing the original rise: negative feedback.
distractorRationale.d: Shivering raises temperature, opposing the original fall: negative feedback.

questions.explanation: In positive feedback the response amplifies the stimulus that triggered it. Cervical stretch causes oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and further stretches the cervix, until delivery ends the loop. The other examples each oppose the original change.

questions.stem: In a negative feedback loop, what does the integrator use to decide whether a response is needed?

options.text: The difference between the sensed value and the set point (the error signal)
The absolute value of the effector output alone
The rate of the afferent nerve impulses only, without a reference value
The size of the perturbation before it reaches the sensor

questions.correctOptionText: The difference between the sensed value and the set point (the error signal)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the integrator compares the sensor signal with the set point and responds to the difference.
distractorRationale.b: Effector output is the result of the decision, not its input.
distractorRationale.c: A signal without a reference value cannot define an error.
distractorRationale.d: The integrator acts on what the sensor detects, not on the unobserved disturbance.

questions.explanation: A feedback loop can only respond to a deviation it has detected. The integrator compares the sensed value with its set point and produces an error signal, which determines the size of the effector response.

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate meal, plasma glucose rises, beta cells in the pancreas release insulin, and glucose uptake into muscle and fat increases so plasma glucose falls. Which statement correctly classifies this?

options.text: Negative feedback: the response opposes the rise in glucose, with beta cells as sensor and integrator and tissues as effectors
Positive feedback: the response removes the stimulus
Positive feedback: insulin raises glucose further
Feedforward only: there is no detection of the glucose rise

questions.correctOptionText: Negative feedback: the response opposes the rise in glucose, with beta cells as sensor and integrator and tissues as effectors

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta cells detect glucose directly and respond in proportion, and the tissue response lowers glucose back towards its set point.
distractorRationale.b: Removing the stimulus is the hallmark of negative, not positive, feedback.
distractorRationale.c: Insulin lowers plasma glucose, not raises it.
distractorRationale.d: Beta cells sense glucose directly, so detection of the perturbation does occur.

questions.explanation: The deviation (raised glucose) is detected by beta cells, which release insulin. Insulin drives glucose uptake and storage, reducing plasma glucose and so the stimulus for insulin release. Because the response opposes the original change, it is negative feedback.

questions.stem: True or false: A negative feedback loop holds the regulated variable exactly at its set point with no residual deviation.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A feedback loop can respond only after a deviation has been detected, so some error always remains. The size of the residual error is expressed by the gain, which is finite for any real control system.

questions.stem: Two control systems face the same disturbance. System X leaves a residual error that is large compared with the correction it achieves; system Y leaves a residual error that is small compared with its correction. Which statement about their gains (quoted as positive magnitudes) is correct?

options.text: System Y has the higher gain and holds the variable closer to its set point
System X has the higher gain because it leaves more error to correct
Both have the same gain because the disturbance is the same
System Y has infinite gain because its error is small

questions.correctOptionText: System Y has the higher gain and holds the variable closer to its set point

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gain is correction divided by remaining error, so a small residual error relative to the correction means a high gain.
distractorRationale.b: A large residual error makes the denominator large and the gain low.
distractorRationale.c: The gain depends on how much of the disturbance is corrected, not on the disturbance alone.
distractorRationale.d: A real feedback system always leaves some error, so its gain is finite.

questions.explanation: Gain is the correction achieved divided by the error remaining, so the system with the smaller residual error relative to its correction has the higher gain. Because feedback can only act on an error that already exists, no real system has infinite gain.

questions.stem: A glucose load would raise plasma glucose by 6.0 mmol/L if there were no feedback. With insulin-mediated regulation the rise is only 1.5 mmol/L. Calculate the gain, where gain = (uncorrected change - remaining change) / remaining change.
questions.explanation: The correction is 6.0 - 1.5 = 4.5 mmol/L and the remaining error is 1.5 mmol/L. The gain is 4.5 / 1.5 = 3, so the feedback corrects three times the residual deviation. A higher gain would hold glucose closer to its set point.

questions.stem: Using thermoregulation as an example, identify the sensor, integrator and effectors in a negative feedback loop, and explain how a rise in core temperature is detected and corrected.
markingGuide: Sensors: skin and core thermoreceptors, including hypothalamic neurons
Integrator: hypothalamus compares the signal with the set point and produces an error signal
Effectors: sweat glands (evaporative heat loss) and skin arteriolar vasodilation (increased heat loss); reduced heat production
Response opposes the rise, so temperature falls towards the set point
As temperature returns to the set point the sensor signal and response diminish (loop closes)
questions.explanation: Thermoreceptors detect the rise and signal the hypothalamus, which compares it with the set point and activates effectors. Sweating and skin vasodilation increase heat loss, so temperature falls back towards the set point, reducing the stimulus. Because the response opposes the perturbation, this is negative feedback.

questions.stem: Distinguish negative from positive feedback, giving one physiological example of each, and explain why positive feedback is not used to maintain a stable internal environment.
markingGuide: Negative feedback: the response opposes the change, stabilising the variable near a set point
Negative feedback example: thermoregulation, plasma glucose regulation or arterial pressure control
Positive feedback: the response amplifies the change, driving the variable further from the starting point
Positive feedback example: oxytocin and uterine contractions in labour, or the blood clotting cascade
Positive feedback is unstable unless terminated by an external event (delivery, sealing of the vessel)
So it suits rapid all-or-none events, not maintenance of a stable variable
questions.explanation: Negative feedback opposes the deviation and so stabilises a variable, as in thermoregulation. Positive feedback amplifies a change, as with oxytocin in labour or the clotting cascade, and ends only when an external event removes the stimulus. Because it drives the variable away from its start point, it cannot maintain a stable internal environment.

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate meal plasma glucose rises. Describe how this perturbation is detected and corrected, identifying the sensor, integrator and effectors, and explain why the loop leaves a residual error rather than correcting perfectly.
markingGuide: Perturbation: absorbed glucose raises plasma glucose above its set point
Detection: pancreatic beta cells sense the raised glucose directly (sensor, with an integrating function)
Response: insulin is released and acts on effectors, muscle, fat and liver, increasing glucose uptake and storage
Plasma glucose falls, reducing the stimulus for insulin release (negative feedback)
A feedback loop responds only to an error that already exists, so some deviation remains
Gain describes effectiveness: gain = (uncorrected change - remaining change) / remaining change, which is finite
questions.explanation: Beta cells detect the rise in glucose and release insulin, which drives glucose uptake and storage in muscle, fat and liver, so plasma glucose falls and insulin release falls. Because the response is triggered by a deviation that already exists, some error always remains, and the gain quantifies how effectively the loop corrects the disturbance.
